name: Semantic Layers
title: Semantic Layers
answer: A semantic layer defines business terms, metrics and relationships on top of raw tables, so that revenue or active customer means one agreed thing across reports, dashboards and queries. It sits between the physical schema and the people or systems that ask questions of it. Text to SQL systems that use one produce far more consistent answers than systems reading raw column names, because the model chooses from defined metrics and joins instead of guessing at abbreviations. The scope covers dimensions, measures, hierarchies and the join paths that connect them.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A semantic layer is usually stored as metadata, often in YAML, JSON or a modeling language, and served by a semantic layer engine or a business intelligence platform. That engine translates a request into SQL against a warehouse such as PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery or Databricks. Agents reach the layer through an API, a SQL endpoint or a Model Context Protocol server, and this site tracks 2451 active MCP servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses. The definitions themselves live in version control alongside the models they describe.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts and analytics engineers define entities, dimensions, measures and joins in a modeling file, then map each definition to physical columns and tables. They test the definitions against known results, review changes and publish a versioned model. A query from a person or an AI agent is resolved against those definitions, and the engine generates the SQL. This keeps metric logic in one place instead of repeating it across dashboards, notebooks and prompts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Each metric needs an owner, a definition and a documented lineage back to source tables, so that changes can be reviewed and audited. Access controls apply at the semantic layer as well as the warehouse, which lets teams restrict sensitive measures without exposing raw columns. The main risks are stale definitions, conflicting local copies and agents that bypass the layer and query tables directly. Provenance matters when a number is challenged, because the layer can show which definition, join and filter produced it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Semantic layers are becoming the context layer for AI agents that write SQL, with metric definitions acting as guardrails for generated queries. More vendors are exposing their models through MCP and similar interfaces, which lets assistants discover metrics without hardcoded prompts. Automated drafting of definitions from query logs is likely to grow, along with testing of agent output against the layer. The open questions are how to version definitions that agents depend on and how to keep human review in the loop as the number of consumers grows.
